correctness.rationale: The claim quantifies over all s>=3 with positive integer abundances and identical N. The identities for Shannon and inverse Simpson reduce it *exactly* to ordinary partitions of excess k=N-s and two integer invariants. A complete table for k<=7 covers every unbounded s (at most s parts), and exact pairwise comparisons prove identical weak orders for k<=5, exactly two Simpson-tie classes at k=6 with length restrictions, and one strict reversal at k=7. The verified witness uses exact products 746496<800000 and square sums s+41>s+39. For s<=2 a separate monotonicity proof applies. The standalone stdlib checker recomputed every partition class and pair; no extrapolation from finite n was used.

originality.rationale: Hill evenness, Lorenz-incomparability, general collision/Shannon nonidentification and empirical opposite index rankings are acknowledged as prior. The specific first finite positive-count census layers k=6 and k=7, their distinction, their universality across any richness s>=3, and uniqueness at the first reversal were not implied by the inspected qualitative results or matched public mathematical records. Closest available full sources were compared at the level of domain, assumptions and implication, not title. Residual risks: a directly relevant 2002 landscape article was abstract-only, and unindexed finite tables could exist.
residual_risks: The full text of Nagendra (2002) was not accessible; its abstract establishes only qualitative opposite responses but uninspected tables could be relevant.
A complete census of all unindexed literature is not possible; failure to find an identical theorem is not proof of worldwide novelty.
The published mathematical-records database covers only its indexed contents, not all previous literature.

value.rationale: This is a natural minimal-census invariant for two canonical Hill evenness choices in a live ecological measurement debate. It gives a universal exact guarantee that both indices cannot produce opposite assessments with <=6 excess individuals, distinguishes an earlier tie-disagreement threshold of six from strict reversal at seven, and classifies every first extremal pair across arbitrary richness. It is useful as a precise finite-count benchmark and as a warning about index selection even with matched richness and sample sizes. The claim does not require an unsupported ecological causal conclusion, and is not a mere recomputation of a known published table.
